messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia is a 51-year-old Middle Eastern American woman who came to treatment after years of trying to arrange her life around a sense of danger she could never fully explain to other people. She is divorced and works as a social ministry worker, a role that asks her to meet with vulnerable families, sit with them in private offices, and move through shelters, church basements, and community buildings where doors open and close behind her all day. In childhood, the person who physically abused her was a caregiver inside her own home, and what remains most vivid is not a story she can tell from beginning to end, but the bodily certainty of being trapped with an adult who could turn on her without warning.

When Nadia speaks about those years, her words thin out and then stop. She says she knows what happened, but she “can’t get it into language right.” Instead, memory arrives in fragments that take hold of her body before she has time to think. She will suddenly feel herself pulled back into the same position she was in then—shoulders tightened, body braced, attention fixed on where the door is and whether she can get to it. What comes with those moments is not sadness so much as a surge of furious heat. She has said more than once that whenever the past comes close, what floods her is rage: rage at the caregiver, rage at being small, rage at having had nowhere to go.

Over time, she built a life that tried to prevent any repetition of that trapped feeling. Even now, in ordinary settings, Nadia often reacts as though danger is already present. If someone steps into a hallway behind her, if a door shuts suddenly, if she realizes she is in a room with one other person and no easy exit, her body responds before she can reason with it. She turns quickly, scans, looks behind her again, then again, checking whether someone is following or approaching. She knows there are many moments when “nothing is actually wrong,” but that knowledge does not stop the jolt. What frightens her most is how instantly she can feel cornered.

At work, these habits have become woven into her day. Nadia tries to position herself near exits in every room she enters. In case conferences she chooses the chair closest to the door and keeps part of her attention on the hallway outside. During home visits and meetings with male parishioners or clients, she has become adamant about not being alone with another person; she finds reasons to keep a colleague nearby, leave a door open, or move the conversation into a more public area. She experiences these choices as necessary, not excessive. To her, being alone behind a closed door with one other person carries the old logic of childhood: once the door is closed, anything can happen and no one will know.

The cost has grown more visible over the past year. Nadia has begun avoiding work itself on some days, especially when her schedule includes one-on-one meetings in unfamiliar settings. She has called out, rearranged appointments, or lingered outside buildings trying to steady herself before going in. Coworkers have noticed that she is tense and easily angered. When someone startles her from behind or questions why she needs a certain seat, she can snap sharply, her voice rising with an intensity that surprises even her. Later she feels embarrassed, but in the moment it feels as if she is defending herself against something immediate. The same vigilance follows her outside work; she checks behind her in parking lots, in grocery store aisles, even walking from her car to her apartment.

Nadia’s divorce is part of the background of her life now rather than something she centers, but she describes a long-standing difficulty tolerating confinement, unpredictability, and the feeling of being alone with someone who has power over the atmosphere in a room. She has become increasingly aware that much of her day is organized around preventing that feeling from arising. Still, she has not experienced these patterns as symptoms so much as precautions that make sense.

What finally brought her to seek help was a recent incident at work. She was meeting with a client in a small office when the client shifted in his chair and the door clicked more firmly shut. Nadia instantly felt her body lock into that old posture, as if she were back in the room where the abuse happened. She could not find words for what was happening; all she knew was that she was furious, on edge, and desperate to get out. She ended the meeting abruptly and spent the rest of the day shaken and humiliated. Coming to treatment, Nadia says she wants to be able to do her job without feeling hunted or trapped. At the same time, she is afraid that if she lets herself come closer to the memories, the rage in them will be too much to contain.
